3.2.4.2 Forecasting of Crop Area and Production

The scheme aims to provide advance information on season-wise area and production of certain principal crops before the final data of area under crops is settled during Jamabandhi and the final yield rates as per the Crop Cutting Experiments (CCE) become available. The advance estimates of area and production of 56 principal food and non-food crops are worked out for the State based on the Team Meetings conducted at the District/State level, and the reports are furnished to the Government.

3.2.4.3 Crop Estimation Survey on Principal Crops

To estimate the average yield per hectare and total production of principal crops, the Directorate of Economics and Statistics conducts Crop Cutting Experiments in coordination with the Agriculture Department.

Under the General Crop Estimation Survey, Crop Cutting Experiments are conducted every Fasli year for 24 food and non-food crops

123

(Paddy, Cholam, Cumbu, Ragi, Maize, Varagu, Redgram, Blackgram, Greengram, Horsegram, Samai, Cowpea, Cotton, Sugarcane, Gingelly, Groundnut, Sunflower, Thinai, Panivaragu, Kuthiraivali, Bengalgram, Castor, Soyabean and Mochai). The data is uploaded through the Digital General Crop Estimation Survey (DGCES) App of the Government of India. Based on the data uploaded through the DGCES App, estimates of average yield per hectare and total production are arrived at and submitted to the Government.

During the year 2025-2026, a total number of 9,524 Crop Cutting Experiments have been planned and are being conducted in the Districts. For the year 2026-2027, there are 9,724 Crop Cutting Experiments have been planned.

3.2.4.4 Crop Cutting Experiments for Fruits and Vegetables

A Crop Cutting Experiment (CCE) is a scientific method used to estimate the average yield of a crop. In this method, a small, randomly selected plot in a field is harvested and the produce is weighed. The result is then used to estimate crop yield per hectare for a larger area.

124

CCEs are useful for preparing crop production statistics, assessing crop losses, and determining crop insurance compensation.

Under the Fruits and Vegetables Estimation Scheme, this Directorate conducts Crop Cutting Experiments every Fasli year for 8 fruit crops viz., Banana, Mango, Jack, Guava, Grapes, Orange, Lemon and Pineapple and 5 vegetable crops viz., Sweet Potato, Brinjal, Lady’s finger, Cabbage and Tomato. Estimates of average yield and production are arrived at based on the data collected through these experiments.

11. Sustainable Development Goals

Tamil Nadu is committed to achieving inclusive and sustainable economic growth in line with its vision of becoming a 1.5 Trillion Dollar Economy by 2036. The Department of Sericulture

32

The Department contributes directly and indirectly to the achievement of the following Sustainable Development Goals:

Goal 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

Sericulture, being an agro-based micro and small-scale rural industry, provides continuous employment and livelihood opportunities, particularly to rural people, through mulberry cultivation, cocoon production, silk reeling and allied activities.

More than 60% of the farm labourers engaged in sericulture activities are women. The sector provides them with employment and income opportunities, thereby improving their economic well-being and contributing to family welfare. It also supports rural incomes and strengthens economic activity in rural areas.

During 2025–2026, 3,050 new beneficiaries were brought under sericulture through the Silk

4.1.7 Duplicate Bill number/Token number

In IFHRMS, once ‘Initiator’ creates a bill, Bill number (16 digit) and on its approval Token number (16 digit) is automatically generated by the system. Each bill should, therefore, have a unique Bill number and a unique Token number.

Data analysis, however, disclosed that 3,456 bills generated in IFHRMS had the same bill number for two different bills. Similarly, 860 bills submitted during this period had the same token number for two different bills. This affects credibility of data generated through IFHRMS.

The Government while accepting the observation stated (January 2023) that bill/token numbers gets duplicated in some instances due to occasional server slowness. To resolve this issue system has been updated to handle one bill at a time for one DDO with validation of last bill number plus one.

4.1.12 Issues in Rejection of bills

Bills presented online by DDOs are checked against the audit points in PAOs/Treasuries at three levels (i.e. L1, L2 and L3) before being approved for payment. If a bill is fit for rejection, L1 notes the objection in remarks field and forwards the bill to L2 and further to L3, who can either overrule the objections raised and pass the bill for payment or can reject the bill after recording his reasons in remarks column. Once the bill is rejected, DDO is

Audit observed the following shortcomings in rejection of bills:

 IFHRMS did not generate TNTC ‘Form 69’ listing the audit points which the bill failed to satisfy. Instead, audit points were manually written in physical ‘Form 69’ and enclosed with hard copy of rejected bill sent to DDO.

 Bills could be rejected even if L1, L2 and L3 auditors do not record any reasons in their respective remarks field as it was not made mandatory. Data analysis revealed that 26,153 bills, rejected during 2021-22, did not carry any remarks.

 Due to lack of a standardised list of reasons for rejecting a bill, L1, L2 and L3 auditors record meaningless reasons in their remarks field viz., ‘l’, ‘j’, ‘k’, audit, reject, etc. This did not help DDOs to readily understand rejection reasons and take remedial action.

 Non-recording of rejection reasons by L1 and/or L2 meant that L2/L3 could not take appropriate action within the system itself and must rely on physical bills.

 In 555 bills, despite L1 remarks rejecting the bills, L2/L3 auditors overruled L1 remarks and passed bills for payment, without recording their remarks, as it was not mandatory. Thus, in 555 cases reasons for overruling L1 remarks were not recorded in the system.

Non-generation of ‘Form 69’ in IFHRMS and non-mandatory remarks field for recording bill rejection reasons meant that DDOs had to wait for physical copies of bills and enclosures from PAOs/Treasuries to know the reason for bill rejection and take corrective action, which defeats the goal of paperless environment.
